# snowglobe

> snowglobe is a Go CLI that turns a Docker image into a static website that runs it in the
> browser: real Linux on a 64-bit ARM CPU emulated in WebAssembly (armless), restored from a
> snapshot taken once the app was ready. The output is a folder of static files (GitHub Pages
> works); no server runs the program. The same site also runs headlessly from the command line,
> in a container or natively with no Docker (the emulator sandboxes itself), as a single
> executable, and as a sandbox that agents and job runners drive, on machines without KVM.
> Guests must be arm64 Alpine images (FROM alpine, built for arm64, or FROM arm64v8/alpine).

Live demos: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/ (Supabase, Elixir IEx, PostgreSQL,
Elixir + Postgres, Python + Rich, TypeScript + Zod, Go + Bubble Tea, Rust + clap, Java + Gson,
curl + jq, DuckDB). Docs: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/docs/ (guides and the full CLI
reference). Source: https://github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe

Install: a release binary (Linux x86-64 or arm64, macOS on Apple silicon; one file that carries
its own snowglobe-vm, unpacked into the cache on first native use) from
https://github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe/releases, or
`curl -fsSL https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/install.sh | sh` (checks the release's
SHA256SUMS, installs to ~/.local/bin; `SNOWGLOBE_VERSION`, `SNOWGLOBE_INSTALL_DIR`), or
`go install github.com/filipecabaco/snowglobe/cmd/snowglobe@latest`.

## Commands

- `snowglobe build <dir with a Dockerfile | image ref | image archive> [flags]` builds the site
  into `--out` (default `dist`). With Docker by default; `--builder native` (or
  `SNOWGLOBE_BUILDER=native`) needs no Docker: it pulls the image from its registry (Docker Hub,
  GHCR, any registry serving public images) or reads a `docker save` / OCI layout archive.
- `snowglobe serve [dir] [--port N]` previews a built site on localhost.
- `snowglobe pool <dir>` makes every site under a directory share one content-addressed blob store.
- `snowglobe pwa <site> [--name N] [--short-name N]` makes a built site an installable Progressive
  Web App that works offline once it has run. Run it after `pool`.
- `snowglobe agent-pages <dir>` puts every `--agent` site under a directory on the agent page,
  `<dir>/agent/` (its `runtimes.json`, scripts and service worker; the page is the demo site's
  `site/agent/index.html`). Sites built from the same source are one machine (the one named after
  it). Run it after `pool` and `pwa`.
- `snowglobe pack <site> [-o site.tar.gz]` writes a site as one self-contained tarball (.tar.gz or
  .tar.zst, pooled blobs included) to publish on a CDN.
- `snowglobe run [site] [--name N] [--detach] [--runtime docker|native]` restores a built site
  headlessly. `docker` (the default) is a sandboxed container (unprivileged, read-only,
  memory-capped, offline unless built with a network); `native` (or `SNOWGLOBE_RUNTIME=native`, and
  whenever there is no Docker) runs snowglobe-vm here, which sandboxes itself: no_new_privs,
  Landlock and seccomp on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS. In a terminal it is an interactive session
  (ctrl-] quits); with stdin piped, each line is typed in as a command and the output printed as
  plain text. The site can be a directory, a tarball, a tarball URL, or a deployed site's URL
  (e.g. https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/python/), fetched into a local cache first.
  Native instances of one site share its snapshot's memory: the first writes it to an image in
  the cache (`ram/`, one per snapshot, named by its hash) and every instance maps it
  copy-on-write, so pages no instance writes are held once and a restore takes a few
  milliseconds (Linux: ~46 MB PSS per Python instance instead of ~111 MB).
  `SNOWGLOBE_RAM_IMAGE=off` restores into memory of the instance's own.
  - `-p HOST:GUEST` (repeatable) forwards a host port to a guest port (127.0.0.1 unless
    IP:HOST:GUEST); needs a site built with `--network fetch`.
  - `--max-runtime DURATION` ends the run after that long (exit 124); `--stop-file PATH` ends it
    once PATH exists (exit 143). Either way the job running in the guest is killed first.
  - `--log-dir DIR` keeps durable logs: `console.log` (the app's terminal), `serial.log` (kernel
    messages, the job shell) and `events.jsonl` (start, restored, job_start, job_end, stop; one
    JSON object a line). Named native instances log to the user cache's `snowglobe/logs/<name>`.
  - `--tunnel [HOST:]PORT=URL`, `--tunnel-token URL`, `--allow-private`, `--record-reads FILE`.
  - `--fork` (with `--detach --name`, native) makes the instance a template: it restores once,
    and every `snowglobe sh` on it runs in a fresh copy of the machine, forked in milliseconds and
    sharing its memory. Nothing one command does is seen by the next; `sh` is all it takes.
- `snowglobe exec <name> <command>` types one command into a running instance's app and prints
  only what it printed (plain text when piped): the way to drive a REPL.
- `snowglobe sh <name> [--json] [--timeout SECS] '<command>'` runs a shell command, passed as one
  quoted argument (its own flags would otherwise be read as snowglobe's), on a native
  instance's serial root shell, whatever its app is, with the app's environment, starting in the
  home directory (`$EXCLAVE_WORKSPACE` is a scratch directory of its own): its output and
  exit status (`{"exit", "output", "timed_out", "killed"}` with `--json`). Out of time (default
  300 s), the command and everything it started are killed (exit 124).
- `snowglobe cp <src> <dst>` copies files or directories in or out of a native instance
  (`name:/path` on one side).
- `snowglobe mcp <site | url> [--name N] [--keep] [--log-dir DIR]` serves a site to an agent as an
  MCP server over stdio: an isolated Linux machine with `run_command` (with `timeout_seconds`),
  `write_file` and `read_file`. No Docker, KVM or privileges. Example:
  `claude mcp add sandbox -- snowglobe mcp https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/python/`
- `snowglobe mcp --daemon` serves the daemon to an agent over MCP (stdio): `status`,
  `list_templates`, `add_template`, `remove_template`, `list_machines`, `up`, `stop_machine`,
  `run_command` (on a `machine`, a fresh fork of a `template`, or a `service`'s replica),
  `write_file`, `read_file`, `snapshot_machine`, `list_snapshots`, `remove_snapshot`,
  `list_services`, `add_service`, `remove_service`, `build` (waits by default), `build_status`,
  `list_builds`, `cancel_build`, `submit_run`, `run_status` (`wait_seconds`), `list_runs`,
  `list_ports`, `check_port`, `recent_events`, `fleet_diff`, `fleet_plan`, `fleet_apply` (one
  `step` too), `graph`, `list_links`, `link`, `unlink`, and fleets kept like compose projects:
  `list_fleets`, `add_fleet`, `write_fleet`, `read_fleet`, `apply_fleet`, `start_instance`,
  `stop_instance`, `forget_fleet`. Example:
  `claude mcp add snowglobe -- snowglobe mcp --daemon`
- `snowglobe bundle <site | url> [-o FILE] [--target linux|darwin] [--runtime snowglobe-vm]`
  makes a site one executable (snowglobe-vm with the site appended) that takes `run`'s flags, plus
  one-shot jobs: `--workspace DIR --cmd COMMAND [--env K=V] [--env-file JSON] [--timeout SECS]`
  writes DIR into a fresh machine, runs the command, and returns its output, exit status and
  `out/`. `--serve SOCKET --jobs-root DIR` restores once and forks per job; `--server SOCKET` is
  its client.
- `snowglobe daemon [--listen ADDR --token-file F] [--detach]` is the orchestrator: it keeps templates (a
  site restored once) and machines forked from them, with an HTTP/JSON API on a Unix socket in the
  user cache (`/v1/templates`, `/v1/machines`, `/v1/machines/{name}/jobs`,
  `/v1/templates/{name}/jobs` for a job on a fresh fork), and over TCP for requests bearing the
  token with `--listen`. `SNOWGLOBE_DAEMON=http://HOST:PORT` and `SNOWGLOBE_DAEMON_TOKEN` point
  the CLI at a remote one. Nothing it starts outlives it: stopped (ctrl-c, SIGTERM, `snowglobe
  daemon stop`; a second ctrl-c skips the grace), it stops its template servers, machines and builds; killed outright, they stop
  themselves (each holds a lifeline to it). Started again, it restores its templates from their
  sites and starts its services' replicas; machines are not brought back.
  It builds too: `POST /v1/builds {"name","source"|"dockerfile","network","memory_mb","cpus",
  "builder","no_template"}` runs `snowglobe build` (a directory by its full path, an image
  reference, or a Dockerfile's text; Docker when there, else natively for images) and makes the
  site a template; `GET /v1/builds`, `/v1/builds/{id}`, `/v1/builds/{id}/log?follow=1&offset=N`,
  `DELETE /v1/builds/{id}` (cancels, or removes a finished one). A machine's terminal is a WebSocket
  at `/v1/machines/{name}/attach?rows=R&cols=C`. `/v1/metrics?since=MS` is a sample every 5 s for
  an hour (memory, machines, replicas, jobs, latencies) and totals; `/metrics` is Prometheus text.
- `snowglobe template add <site> [--name T] [--max-machines N] [--idle 30m]`, `template ls`,
  `template rm T` (removes its machines too). `--idle` stops the template's server after that long
  with no machine; the next `up` or job restores it (about a second).
- `snowglobe daemon --memory 8G [--wait 30s]` caps what templates and machines take together: a
  machine that doesn't fit waits for room, then is refused (429) with the reason. `up --ttl 1h`
  stops a machine after that long.
- `snowglobe up <template> [--name N] [-p [IP:][HOST:]GUEST]... [--label K=V]...` forks a machine
  in tens of milliseconds, sharing the template's memory: it lasts until stopped, keeps what it
  writes, and the daemon forwards its ports (-p 8000 picks a host port). `sh`, `cp`, `exec`,
  `attach`, `ps` and `stop` reach the daemon's machines like instances.
- `snowglobe snapshot save <machine> [--name S]` saves a machine whole (memory, running processes,
  the files it wrote); `up <template> --snapshot S` starts a machine from it, and
  `template add --snapshot S [--name T]` makes it a template, every machine of which starts there.
  `snapshot ls`, `snapshot rm S`.
- `snowglobe service add <name> --template T [-p [IP:]HOST:GUEST]... [--min 0] [--max 1]
  [--idle 5m] [--concurrency 10] [--state discard|keep]` puts a template's machines behind host
  ports the daemon holds: each connection (or `sh <name>`) goes to a replica started on demand.
  `--min 0` scales to zero: replicas idle for `--idle` stop, and the next request forks one (about
  20 ms to the first answer when the template is a snapshot with its server listening).
  `--state keep` saves the replica before it stops and the next one carries on (max 1);
  `discard` starts each from the template. `service ls`, `service rm <name>`; API
  `/v1/services`, `/v1/services/{name}/jobs`.
- `snowglobe daemon --detach` starts the daemon in the background, in a session of its own so it
  outlives the terminal, its log in `daemon.log` beside the socket; it returns once the daemon
  answers, and does nothing if one runs. `snowglobe daemon stop` stops it, and everything it
  started, and returns once they have stopped.
- `snowglobe ui [--port 7777] [--no-open] [--start-daemon]` serves the daemon in a browser on 127.0.0.1
  (the link carries a session token; `--start-daemon` starts a detached daemon first when none runs),
  one view at a time: Overview (the last hour on one time axis, a lane per template with machine
  lifespans), Network (the plan's templates and links dotted, then a group per fleet instance with its
  machines, solid edges where one really reaches another by name, and each host port it opens; drag
  one node onto another to link them), Fleets (each fleet file, its instances, its plan as steps that
  each apply on their own, and an editor for the file), Machines (one control per task, and the
  templates, machines, services, ports and snapshots), Run (a command on a fresh fork) and Builds. A
  terminal on any machine is ghostty-web over `/v1/machines/{name}/attach`. The page is Preact + htm,
  served gzipped from inside the binary, with no build step.
- Links: nothing joins the daemon's machines but a link. `POST /v1/links {"from","to","port","as",
  "as_port"}` lets a machine, or every machine of a template, reach a machine, a service (one of its
  replicas, started if none runs) or a template's machines as `as:as_port`; `GET /v1/links`,
  `DELETE /v1/links/{name}`. Each source machine gets a Unix socket of its own per link (mode 0600,
  in its template's socket directory), so no TCP port opens on the host, and links work under egress
  `none`. `GET /v1/graph` returns nodes (templates, services, machines, ports, snapshots, with fleet
  and instance) and edges (fork, replica, serves, link, reach, port, saved, made). MCP: `graph`,
  `list_links`, `link`, `unlink`.
- `snowglobe submit <template> '<cmd>' [--timeout S] [--env K=V]...` is fire and forget: the
  command runs once on a fresh fork, thrown away after, and the run's id is printed at once.
  `snowglobe runs [<id> [--wait]] [--json]` lists runs or shows one's output and exit status
  (`--wait` exits with it). API: `POST /v1/runs {"template","cmd","env","timeout"}`,
  `GET /v1/runs`, `GET /v1/runs/{id}`.
- `snowglobe ports [--json]` lists the host ports the daemon holds and where each leads (machine
  or service, guest port, open or at zero); `snowglobe ports check <port> [--ip IP]` says whether
  one is free or what holds it (exit 1 when taken). API: `/v1/ports`, `/v1/ports/check?port=N`.
- `snowglobe events [--json] [--after SEQ]` streams the daemon's events (kind, subject, message:
  machine.up, machine.stopped, machine.expired, service.replica_up, template.asleep,
  template.awake, snapshot.saved, admission.refused, ...), the last 200 first; `snowglobe top
  [--once]` shows it live (memory and budget, templates, services, machines, recent events). API:
  `/v1/events` (server-sent events, `?after=SEQ`), `/v1/stats`.
- `snowglobe apply [-f snowglobe.toml]` gets the daemon to what a fleet file says: `[templates.N]`
  (`site`, or `build` = a Dockerfile directory built first with optional `network`, or `snapshot`;
  `idle`, `max_machines`, `egress` = none (the default) | internet | private, `expose` = guest ports
  the others reach under mode all), `[network]` (`mode` = exclusive (the default: each instance
  reaches only its own machines) | inclusive (every machine of a template reaches the target's
  template's, across instances) | all (as inclusive, plus every template reaches every other's
  `expose`d ports by its name)), `[links.N]` (`from`, `to` = a template, service or machine of the
  file, `port`, `as`, `as_port`), `[snapshots.N]` (`template`, `run` = commands that must succeed, `ready`
  = a command retried until it succeeds, `timeout`), `[services.N]` (`template`, `ports`, `min`,
  `max`, `idle`, `concurrency`, `state`, `labels`), `[machines.N]` (`template`, `count`, `ports`,
  `ttl`, `labels`). What changed is replaced with what is made from it; what left the file is
  removed. `snowglobe diff` shows the plan; `snowglobe down [-f F | --name FLEET]` removes it all.
  Examples: examples/fleet/snowglobe.toml, examples/todo-fleet/snowglobe.toml (an Elixir app and
  Postgres, linked as db.internal:5432, egress none).
- Fleets as compose projects: the daemon keeps a list of fleet files. `GET/POST /v1/fleets` (POST
  `{"file"}` adds one where it is; `{"name","text"}` writes a new one, checked before it is saved),
  `GET/PUT/DELETE /v1/fleets/{name}` (GET plans it, `?instance=ID`; DELETE `?down=1` removes what it
  made first), `POST /v1/fleets/{name}/apply {"instance","step"}` (all of the plan, or one step by its
  key once the steps it waits on are done), `POST /v1/fleets/{name}/down`. A fleet runs as
  instances, like `docker compose -p`: templates and snapshots are shared, services, machines and
  links are made per instance (label `snowglobe.instance`); `main` keeps the file's names, another
  gets `-ID` names and host ports the system picks. `POST /v1/fleets/{name}/instances {"instance"}`
  starts one, `DELETE /v1/fleets/{name}/instances/{id}` removes it.
- `snowglobe attach <name>` joins a running instance (ctrl-] detaches); `snowglobe ps` lists them;
  `snowglobe stop <name>` stops one (natively: through its stop file, killing its job and logging
  why).
- `snowglobe warm <site> <reads.json ...>` adds the files runs recorded to the site's warm pack.
- `snowglobe tools` builds or finds the tools image; `snowglobe version`.

## Build flags (and the image labels they override)

- `--cmd CMD`: the program to run (default: the image's ENTRYPOINT + CMD). Drops the image's ready and exercise labels.
- `--ready TEXT` / `snowglobe.ready`: snapshot once this text appears on the console (default: after 5 s of quiet).
- `--title TEXT` / `snowglobe.title`: the page title.
- `--memory MB` / `snowglobe.memory`: guest RAM (default 512).
- `--cpus N` / `snowglobe.cpus`: guest CPUs, 1 to 8 (default 1); each runs in a Web Worker.
- `--exercise CMD` (repeatable) / `snowglobe.exercise` (JSON array): commands typed after the snapshot; the files they read are preloaded.
- `--warm REGEX` / `snowglobe.warm`: extra guest paths to preload.
- `--network fetch` / `snowglobe.network`: give the guest a network (default `none`).
- `--tunnel [HOST:]PORT=URL` (repeatable) / `snowglobe.tunnels`: carry other TCP over a WebSocket.
- `--tunnel-token URL` / `snowglobe.tunnel-token`: a fresh token per tunnel connection, put where the URL says `{token}`.
- `--allow-private`: let the build's snapshot reach loopback and private addresses.
- `--builder docker|native`: build with Docker (default) or with none.
- `--sandbox`: keep the guest's file cache in the snapshot, for bundles and native runs.
- `--no-chunks`: don't split large files into content-defined chunks.
- `--agent` / `snowglobe.agent="true"`: make the machine one of the agent page's, `/agent/` (below). Off by default. With `snowglobe.agent-purpose` (one line: what it is good for) and `snowglobe.agent-sample` (a command to try), the page lists it.
- `--agent-exposed-to ORIGIN` (repeatable) / `snowglobe.agent-exposed-to` (JSON array): also share the agent page's WebMCP tools with these https origins (default: none). The page shares its one set of tools with an origin only if every one of its machines does.

Example Dockerfile labels:

    LABEL snowglobe.title="My app" snowglobe.ready="iex(1)> " snowglobe.memory="640" \
          snowglobe.network="fetch" snowglobe.exercise='["h Enum.map"]'

## The agent page (`/agent/`)

One page for agents, with every agent runtime of the site in it: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/agent/
Each runtime is a Linux machine (arm64) that runs in the tab, in a Web Worker of its own; nothing
runs on a server, and the page is static files. Its headline: an agent builds a React app on
Supabase in `web`, and the person sees it live in the page's preview, rebuilt after each change,
beside a feed of what the agent changed. `snowglobe agent-pages <dir>` writes its
list of machines (`agent/runtimes.json`, from each site's `run.json`) and its scripts when a site of
several runs is assembled; a site's own page links there ("For agents", `../agent/?runtime=<site>`),
and the old `/agent/<site>/` addresses go there too. `?runtime=<name>` only preselects: nothing
runs because of the address.

- The page has a service worker (`agent/sw.js`). It makes the page cross-origin isolated, which a
  machine on several CPUs needs (`supabase` runs on 2: SharedArrayBuffer), and carries the
  preview's requests. The first visit installs it and reloads once. Where it can't run (no service
  workers, a hard reload), the several-CPU machines are refused with the reason and the others run.
- Machines start lazily: nothing boots until a command (or a copy) needs it. Each shows its
  state: asleep, waking, awake, busy, suspending, or failed (with Retry).
- A few are awake at once: 2 by default ("2 of 2 awake"). The number field "Machines awake at once",
  `set_awake_limit {count}` and `setAwakeLimit(count)` change it, 1 to 8, for this page load; it
  runs nothing, so it asks no one. Each awake machine is about 540 to 740 MB of memory (supabase,
  on 2 CPUs, about 730). Waking another suspends the least recently used idle one first; a busy
  machine (a job, a copy or an open preview in it) is never suspended: the wake waits, and the
  status line says so. A lower limit suspends idle
  machines, least recently used first; busy ones that keep it over the limit are said so, and
  suspended as they finish. Suspends and wakes go one at a time. Idle for 5 minutes, or hidden for
  a minute, a machine is suspended too.
- Suspended, a machine's state is saved in this browser (IndexedDB, a scope per runtime): only a
  suspended machine's state is kept across a reload. What an awake machine did since its last
  suspend is lost on reload, and the browser asks before leaving while there is any. "Start
  fresh…" (always with a confirmation) goes back to the machine as built.
- A machine that fails (it powered off, its worker crashed, a capture hung) is ended at once, its
  job finished as failed; Retry starts it again. When a machine's files can't be fetched (the blob
  store is unreachable), the page says so: "can't reach the machine's files (<url>)".
- Operations on one machine go one at a time, in the order asked: a run asked during a copy waits
  for it; a run beside a running job is refused (one job at a time).
- Every run, copy and preview, by the form, a WebMCP tool or `window.snowglobeAgent`, asks the
  person at the page first, once per page load. In another page's frame the page refuses to run and
  offers no tools. It needs the network: it doesn't work offline.
- For agents that click and type: the form "Run a command" has the combobox "Runtime", the
  textbox "Shell command", and the buttons "Run" and "Cancel". The first run asks the person at
  the page once per page load ("Let agents use these machines?": Allow). The region "Result" holds
  the latest run: "Exit status: N" and "Command output" ending `[exit N]`, `[timed out]` or
  `[stopped]`; "Earlier runs" lists the ones before it, each tagged with its runtime. The status
  line under Run (the one `role=status`) says what is happening. "Earlier runs" also lists what
  agents ran and copied through WebMCP or a script, tagged "by WebMCP" or "by a script". "Copy a file between machines"
  has "From runtime", "From path", "To runtime", "To path", "Copy" and "Cancel copy". The selected
  machine's terminal is under "Show <runtime>'s terminal". "Preview a machine's web server" has
  "Runtime", "Port", "Path", "Open preview" and "Close preview"; the open preview is a frame with
  an address field ("Address in the preview"), "Reload" and "New tab". Beside it (below it on
  narrower screens), "What the agent changed": a list, "Agent activity, newest first", of every
  run, copy, write and build in every machine (filter: "Show", a machine or "All machines"), each
  tagged with its runtime and who asked, its exit status, and in a watched project (web's
  `/root/app`) "Changed N files", each file a disclosure whose diff is a `pre` labelled "Changes to
  <path>". A build entry says "Build N written in S s; the preview reloaded" or "Build N failed",
  with the error. "Watch an agent build" plays a short walkthrough through the same calls (rename
  the app; a `done` column on Supabase and a checkbox for it; an All / Open / Done filter); "Stop
  the walkthrough" stops it between steps.
- `window.snowglobeAgent` (promises): `listRuntimes()` (name, purpose, state, sample, saved),
  `capabilities()`, `status(runtime)`, `runCommand({runtime, command, timeoutSeconds, requestId})`
  → `{jobId, runtime}` at once (wakes or boots the machine first), `readJob(jobId)`,
  `cancelJob(jobId)` (job ids are unique across runtimes), `writeFile({runtime, path, content})` →
  `{bytes, changes}` once written, `copyFile({fromRuntime, fromPath,
  toRuntime, toPath})` → `{bytes, sha256, readSeconds, writeSeconds}`, `cancelCopy()`,
  `suspend(runtime)`, `wake(runtime)`, `startFresh(runtime)` (asks the person), `setAwakeLimit(count)`
  → `{awakeLimit, awake, overLimit}`, `openPreview({runtime, port, path})` → `{url, base, status |
  error}`, `closePreview()`, `preview()`, `unsaved()`, `metrics()`.
- WebMCP tools, registered once where the browser has `document.modelContext` (or a polyfill such
  as MCP-B's `@mcp-b/global`, even one added up to 15 s after the page starts; the first drafts'
  `provideContext` works too): `list_runtimes`; `run_command {runtime, command, timeout_seconds,
  request_id}` returns a job id; `job_status {job_id}` returns its output, ending `[running]`,
  `[exit N]`, `[timed out]` or `[stopped]` (in a watched project, then `[changed in <dir>: <files>]`);
  `cancel_job {job_id}`; `write_file {runtime, path, content}` writes a UTF-8 text file (at most
  1 MiB; its directory is made) with no shell quoting, as a job in its turn, and returns once it is
  written, with what changed; `copy_file {from_runtime,
  from_path, to_runtime, to_path}` returns the bytes copied and their sha256 (a client's cancel
  signal stops it); `open_preview {runtime, port, path}` opens the page's preview on a server in a
  machine and returns its address and what its first request got; `close_preview`;
  `set_awake_limit {count}` (1 to 8); `list_runtimes` reports `awake_limit`, `preview_base` and
  the open `preview`. The first run, copy or preview asks the person at the page.
- Jobs: one at a time in each machine, as root on its serial shell (never the visible terminal),
  from `/root`, so relative paths work and files persist between jobs. Default timeout 300 s, at
  most 3600; out of time or cancelled, everything the command started is killed. A repeated
  `requestId` returns the same job. Jobs run with `NO_COLOR=1` and `TERM=dumb`; escape sequences
  are stripped from their output.
- Copies: one file, binary-safe, at most 8 MiB, checked by sha256 on both ends; the target is
  replaced only once its copy checks out (its directory is made). It goes over the machines'
  serial lines as base64, so it is slow: tens of KiB a second. Cancellable.
- Watched projects: a machine whose image has the label `snowglobe.agent-watch=<dir>` (web:
  `/root/app`) reports, after each command, the files under `<dir>` it added, changed or deleted
  (`node_modules`, `dist` and `.git` aside), with a unified diff of each (at most 40 files, 300
  lines a file; none for binary files or files over 256 KiB). The diff is measured against a copy
  the machine keeps (`/var/lib/snowglobe/watch/<dir>`), taken before the first command and brought
  up to date after each; the report is taken out of the job's output, so the output is the
  command's own. `readJob` gives it as `changes: {files: [{status, path, diff, added, removed}], more}`.

### The preview

A server in a machine, seen in the page, over HTTP/1.1 (no WebSockets). Its address is

    <preview_base><runtime>/<port>/<path>      preview_base: https://filipecabaco.github.io/snowglobe/agent/preview/

The page's service worker hands each request under it to the agent page, which opens a TCP
connection to `<port>` on the machine's network address, writes the request (Connection: close),
and streams the answer back: a length, chunked, or to the close; binary as it is. A redirect's
Location on the server (`/login`, `http://localhost:<port>/...`) stays inside the preview.
Cookies a server sets are not kept (a service worker can't set them): use tokens, as supabase-js
does. A port with nothing listening answers 502, "Nothing is listening".

- A server must listen on `0.0.0.0`, not `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` (the page connects from outside
  the machine): `serve --watch dist 4173` on `web` (running from its boot), `vite preview --host
  0.0.0.0`, Bun with `hostname: "0.0.0.0"`.
- Live reload without WebSockets: `serve --watch` runs Vite's build in watch mode and answers
  `GET /__build` with `{version, state: "building" | "ok" | "error", error, ms, at}`. While a
  preview is open the page reads it (every 0.5 s for 45 s after a command in that machine, every
  5 s otherwise) and reloads the preview when a new build is written; a failed build is shown in
  the feed and the preview keeps the last page that built. A server with no `/__build` (plain
  `serve dist`, `vite preview`) has the preview reloaded after each command in its machine. Vite's
  dev server and hot module reload don't work in the preview (they need a WebSocket).
- Build pages with relative asset paths: they are served under a prefix. The `web` project's Vite
  config has `base: "./"`.
- The page in the preview is this site's own (same origin): it reaches any machine's server at
  `<preview_base><runtime>/<port>/`. Supabase's API is on port 54321 of `supabase` (Postgres,
  PostgREST and Auth; `/rest/v1` and `/auth/v1`), so supabase-js's URL is
  `<preview_base>supabase/54321`, and its key is `$ANON_KEY` on `supabase`. From inside the page:
  `location.href.split("/preview/")[0] + "/preview/supabase/54321"`.
- A machine with the preview open, and every machine the page in it reaches, is busy: never
  suspended until the preview is closed. One preview at a time. The machines a preview uses count
  as one against the awake limit: a machine the page reaches is woken even beyond the limit, beside
  the preview's own (so `web` and `supabase` together work at any limit). When every awake machine
  is busy with something else (a job, a copy), a preview request or `open_preview` waits up to 30 s
  for one to be free, then fails: 503 "No machine slot free" (raise the awake limit, or close the
  preview).
- Answered only while a preview is open and the person has allowed the page; a preview address
  opened from anywhere but the agent page (typed in, linked from another site) is refused (403).

### Building a web app on Supabase, seen live

Both machines come ready and connected. `supabase` has a `notes` table (`id`, `user_id` default
`auth.uid()`, `body`, `created_at`) with row level security: a user reads, adds and deletes only
their own. `web` has a React app in `/root/app` (Vite 8, React 19, `@supabase/supabase-js`, all
installed: no network needed) that signs up, logs in, lists, adds and deletes notes; from its boot
`serve --watch dist 4173` builds it, serves it, and builds it again on every change.

1. `open_preview {runtime: "web", port: 4173}`: the app, live. supabase-js's URL is
   `<preview_base>supabase/54321` (`src/supabase.js` works it out from the page's address), and its
   key is in `/root/app/.env` (`VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`: the Supabase CLI's fixed local key, which
   is `$ANON_KEY` on `supabase`).
2. Change the app: `write_file {runtime: "web", path: "/root/app/src/App.jsx", content: ...}` (or
   `run_command` with sed). Files: `src/App.jsx` (the app), `src/supabase.js` (the client),
   `src/styles.css`, `index.html`. The page shows the diff, `web` rebuilds (a few seconds natively,
   longer in the tab, where the build runs in the emulated machine), and the preview reloads; a build error shows in the feed, and `wget -qO- 127.0.0.1:4173/__build` on
   `web` says it too.
3. Change the schema on `supabase` with psql, then `notify pgrst, 'reload schema'` so the Data API
   sees it, for example:

       psql "$DB_URL" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 <<'SQL'
       alter table public.notes add column if not exists done boolean not null default false;
       create policy "update own notes" on public.notes for update to authenticated
         using ((select auth.uid()) = user_id) with check ((select auth.uid()) = user_id);
       notify pgrst, 'reload schema';
       SQL

4. On `supabase`: `psql "$DB_URL" -c "select n.id, n.body, u.email from notes n join auth.users u
   on u.id = n.user_id"` shows what the person added in the preview, with their user.

Without a second machine: copy the built `dist` (as a tarball, `copy_file`) to `supabase` and serve
it there with Bun (`BUN_BE_BUN=1 supabase run serve.ts`, `Bun.serve({hostname: "0.0.0.0", port:
3000, ...})`), then `open_preview {runtime: "supabase", port: 3000}`.

### The runtimes on this site

- runtime `supabase`: Supabase for web app building: Postgres, Auth and the Data API, with a preview (2 CPUs; the API on port 54321; `$DB_URL`, `$API_URL`, `$ANON_KEY` in every shell; try `psql "$DB_URL" -c "select now()"`)
- runtime `web`: build web apps: a React app on Supabase, rebuilt and served on port 4173 as it changes (Vite, Node) (the app in `/root/app`, watched: each command's changes are reported; try `cd /root/app && sed -i 's/<h1>Notes/<h1>My notes/' src/App.jsx`)
- runtime `python`: run Python: scripts, numpy and pandas for data work (try `python3 -c 'import numpy, pandas; print(numpy.__version__, pandas.__version__)'`)
- runtime `duckdb`: DuckDB for analytics: SQL over CSV, Parquet and JSON files (try `duckdb -c 'select 6 * 7'`)
- runtime `postgres`: PostgreSQL for database work: load CSV files and query them with psql (try `psql -h /run/postgresql -U postgres -tAc 'select count(*) from planets'`)

For example: write `/root/data.csv` in `python`, `copy_file` it to `duckdb`, query it with
`duckdb -csv -c "select count(*) from 'data.csv'"`, export a CSV, and load it into `postgres` with
`psql -h /run/postgresql -U postgres -c "\copy t from '/root/x.csv' csv header"`.

The other runs (IEx, TypeScript, Go, Rust, curl + jq, Elixir + Postgres and Java) are for people,
on the landing page, not on the agent page.

## Networking (`--network fetch`)

Every request leaves as the visitor's own browser request; there is no proxy server.

- HTTP (port 80): each request becomes a fetch().
- HTTPS (port 443): the machine terminates TLS 1.3 itself (armless's web relay) with a per-build CA
  that only the guest trusts, then the request is replayed with fetch("https://...").
- WebSockets (ws://, wss://): the guest's upgrade opens a browser WebSocket; messages pass through.
- Other TCP: only to destinations the site tunnels (`--tunnel`), over a WebSocket.
- In `snowglobe run`, the same requests leave from the host or the container (through
  HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY if set); other TCP connections are made directly; private addresses are
  refused unless `--allow-private`.
- Limits in the browser: CORS applies (servers without it answer 502), no raw TCP or UDP.

## Isolation

The guest is an emulated machine whose only ways out are its terminal, its 9p filesystem (read
from the site, written to memory) and, with a network, the web relay. Around the emulator: in the
browser, the page's sandbox; natively, the process's own sandbox (no new programs or processes,
no files beyond the site, its cache, socket, logs and a job's workspace); in Docker, the container
as well. `SNOWGLOBE_SANDBOX=strict` refuses to run without the whole native sandbox.

The shared memory image is kept from changing under a machine: the cache's `ram/` is 0700 and
its files 0444, written under a temporary name and renamed into place, and checked on the open
descriptor before mapping (a regular file of this user's, no write bits, one link, no symlink);
anything off and the run restores the usual way. A page a machine writes is its own, and every
restore and fork gets fresh randomness (the guest kernel reseeds on it).

## What a built site contains

- `index.html`: the page that restores the snapshot (`?embed` hides the status strip).
- `system/state.bin.zst`: the snapshot; `system/filesystem.json` + blobs: the root filesystem over 9p.
- `system/warm.pack`: files preloaded in one request; `warm-report.json` explains what went in.
- `run.json`: measured facts of the build; `transcript.json`: the exercise commands and their output.
